title: At the Hotel
audio_script:
Receptionist: Hello. What is your name?
Guest: My name is Anna. A-N-N-A.
Receptionist: Where are you from?
Guest: I am from Italy.
Receptionist: What is your room number?
Guest: Room five. Number five.

title: Shopping — Prices
audio_script:
Man: Excuse me, how much is this T-shirt?
Woman: It's twelve dollars.
Man: Do you have a bigger size?
Woman: Yes, here is large.
Man: Thank you.

title: Family Intro
audio_script: Boy: This is my family. This is my mother. She is a teacher. This is my father. He is a driver. I have one sister. She is five years old.

questions.q: How many sisters does the boy have?

title: Time and Day
audio_script:
Woman: What time is it?
Man: It is eight o'clock.
Woman: Is it Monday today?
Man: No, it is Tuesday.

title: At the Cafe
audio_script:
Waiter: Hello, what would you like?
Customer: A coffee, please. And a sandwich.
Waiter: Small or large coffee?
Customer: Small, please.
Waiter: That is six dollars.

title: Directions Simple
audio_script:
Man: Excuse me, where is the bus station?
Woman: Go straight. Then turn left. It is next to the supermarket.
Man: Thank you very much.

title: Train Announcement
audio_script: Announcement: The train to Manchester leaves from platform four at ten fifteen. Please have your tickets ready. The journey takes two hours. Food and drinks are available in carriage three.

title: Weekend Plans
audio_script:
Sarah: What are you doing this weekend?
Tom: I'm going to visit my grandparents. They live near the beach.
Sarah: How are you going there?
Tom: By train. It takes one hour.
Sarah: Have fun!

title: Shopping Return
audio_script:
Customer: Hello, I bought this jacket yesterday but it is too small.
Shop assistant: Do you have the receipt?
Customer: Yes, here it is.
Shop assistant: Would you like a bigger size or a refund?
Customer: A bigger size, please.

title: Doctor Appointment
audio_script:
Receptionist: Hello, City Clinic.
Man: I need to see a doctor tomorrow.
Receptionist: What time would you like? We have nine AM or three PM.
Man: Three PM is good.
Receptionist: What is your name?
Man: John Miller.

title: Weather Forecast
audio_script: Forecast: Tomorrow will be cloudy in the morning. In the afternoon, there will be light rain. The temperature will be fifteen degrees. On Friday, it will be sunny and warm, around twenty-two degrees.

questions.q: What will weather be tomorrow afternoon?

title: Restaurant Order
audio_script:
Waiter: Are you ready to order?
Woman: Yes, I'll have the chicken salad and orange juice.
Waiter: Anything else?
Woman: No, that's all.
Waiter: The salad is twelve pounds and the juice is three pounds.

title: Travel Problems
audio_script:
Host: Today we talk about travel. Have you ever missed a flight?
Guest: Yes, last year I was travelling to Berlin for a conference. My train to the airport was delayed because of heavy snow, so I arrived late. I had to buy a new ticket and wait six hours for the next flight. I learned to always leave early in winter.
Host: Good advice!

title: University Life
audio_script: Student: I moved to the university dormitory last month. At first it was difficult because I had never lived away from my family before. I had to cook and do laundry myself. But now I have made many friends on my floor and we study together in the evenings. My grades have improved since then.

title: Job Interview Advice
audio_script: Speaker: If you want to succeed in a job interview, you should research the company before you go. Think about why you want to work there and prepare examples of your skills. During the interview, listen carefully and don't speak too quickly. And remember to ask a question at the end.

title: Healthy Lifestyle
audio_script: Doctor: Many people think they need to go to the gym every day to stay healthy, but that's not true. Walking for thirty minutes a day and eating more vegetables can make a big difference. Also, sleeping seven to eight hours is essential. If you follow these simple habits, you will feel much better within a few weeks.

title: Technology in Education
audio_script: Teacher: Since we started using tablets in class, students are more engaged. They can watch videos and do interactive exercises. However, some parents are worried that children spend too much time on screens. We tell them that we limit tablet use to twenty minutes per lesson and encourage outdoor activities.

title: Cultural Festival
audio_script: Guide: Welcome to the spring festival. This tradition started over two hundred years ago when farmers celebrated the end of winter. Today we still wear traditional clothes and dance in the streets. The festival lasts three days and thousands of tourists visit each year.

title: Lecture: Urbanisation
audio_script: Lecturer: Urbanisation is not simply people moving to cities. It involves profound economic and social transformations. In developing countries, the process has been remarkably rapid — what took a century in Europe has happened in three decades in parts of Asia. While this creates opportunities, particularly for young people seeking education, it also puts enormous pressure on housing, transport, and healthcare systems. Governments have struggled to keep pace, and as a result informal settlements have grown dramatically.

questions.q: What point does lecturer make about developing countries?
options: Much faster — 3 decades vs a century
questions.answer: Much faster — 3 decades vs a century

title: News: Remote Work Debate
audio_script: Reporter: The debate over remote work intensified this week after a major tech firm ordered all employees back to the office five days a week. Supporters argue that face-to-face collaboration sparks creativity and builds culture, whereas critics point to studies showing productivity remains stable or even improves at home. Moreover, many workers cite reduced commuting costs and better work-life balance as decisive factors in staying remote. The company's decision has nevertheless been met with resignations.

questions.q: Critics argue remote work productivity is?

title: Interview: Renewable Energy
audio_script:
Interviewer: Is renewable energy now economically viable?
Expert: It is claimed that renewables are still too expensive, but that claim no longer holds. Having fallen by over eighty percent in a decade, solar is now the cheapest source in many regions. Although storage remains a challenge, advances in battery technology are rapidly addressing it. Therefore, the question is no longer if we will transition, but how quickly.

options: Fallen 80% in a decade, now cheapest
questions.answer: Fallen 80% in a decade, now cheapest

title: Discussion: Social Media & Mental Health
audio_script: Psychologist: Research suggests a correlation, not necessarily causation, between heavy social media use and anxiety among teenagers. However, when usage exceeds three hours daily and replaces sleep or face-to-face interaction, the risk increases significantly. Parents should therefore focus less on banning and more on promoting balanced habits and open communication.

title: Lecture: Behavioral Economics
audio_script: Professor: Traditional economics assumes we are rational actors, yet behavioral studies repeatedly show we are predictably irrational. For instance, people will drive twenty minutes to save five dollars on a fifteen-dollar item, but not on a thousand-dollar item, even though the saving is identical. This inconsistency reveals how context, not absolute value, drives decisions.

title: Podcast: Future of Work
audio_script: Host: Automation will not simply eliminate jobs; it will transform them. Roles involving repetitive tasks are most vulnerable, whereas those requiring creativity, emotional intelligence, or complex problem-solving are likely to grow. Consequently, reskilling is no longer optional — it is imperative for both individuals and governments.

title: Panel: AI Ethics
audio_script:
Moderator: Should we anthropomorphise AI?
Panellist 1: We already do — and that's precisely the danger. When a chatbot says 'I understand', users infer empathy where there is only pattern matching. Were we to regulate disclosure more rigorously, we might mitigate deception.
Panellist 2: But regulation alone is insufficient. What concerns me is the accountability vacuum: if an autonomous diagnostic tool errs, who bears liability — the hospital, the developer, or the algorithm itself? Nominally, the institution, but the legal framework hasn't caught up.

options: Users infer empathy where only pattern matching
questions.answer: Users infer empathy where only pattern matching

title: Lecture: Monetary Policy
audio_script: Economist: Conventional wisdom held that low unemployment must drive inflation, yet the post-pandemic period confounded that model. Despite historically tight labour markets, inflation was initially driven by supply-chain disruptions, not wage pressure. The Federal Reserve, having misjudged transitory factors, was compelled to tighten aggressively, albeit at the risk of overtightening. Notwithstanding these challenges, the soft landing narrative has, to date, held.

options: Low unemployment must drive inflation — but inflation came from supply chains
questions.answer: Low unemployment must drive inflation — but inflation came from supply chains

title: Debate: Genetic Editing
audio_script: Speaker: The ethical objection to germline editing often hinges on hubris — the notion that we should not 'play God'. Yet we already intervene extensively in nature. The more substantive concern, to my mind, is equity: were the technology to remain accessible only to the affluent, we risk entrenching a genetic divide that would make current inequalities look trivial. Nevertheless, a blanket prohibition would be equally problematic.

options: Equity — only affluent access → genetic divide
questions.answer: Equity — only affluent access → genetic divide

title: Interview: Architecture & Sustainability
audio_script: Architect: The fetishisation of glass towers is fundamentally at odds with climate goals. A truly sustainable building is not one that merely offsets its carbon, but one that embodies low-embodied-energy materials, passive ventilation, and adaptability over decades. Retrofitting existing stock, unglamorous as it may be, will have far greater impact than any number of flagship 'green' skyscrapers.

title: Documentary: Language Death
audio_script: Narrator: Every forty days, a language dies, taking with it an entire worldview. The process is rarely violent; rather, it is insidious. Parents, believing bilingualism burdens their children, switch to the dominant language. Within two generations, comprehension becomes passive, then vanishes. Documentation, while valuable, is palliative — it preserves a record, not a living tongue.

options: Insidious — parents switch to dominant language
questions.answer: Insidious — parents switch to dominant language

title: Lecture: Cognitive Biases
audio_script: Psychologist: Confirmation bias is not merely seeking agreeable information; it is interpreting ambiguous evidence as supportive. Moreover, we exhibit bias blind spot — recognising bias in others while remaining oblivious to our own. Debiasing, therefore, requires not information but metacognition: the habit of interrogating one's own reasoning.

options: Seeing bias in others but not self
questions.answer: Seeing bias in others but not self

title: Oxford Union: Free Speech
audio_script: Speaker: The paradox of deplatforming is that in attempting to deny a platform to noxious views, we inadvertently platform the very narrative of martyrdom those views crave. Free speech, properly understood, is not the absence of consequences, but the presence of contestation. To sanitise the public square of all discomfort is to infantilise it — and infantilised publics, as history attests, are not resilient but brittle.

options: Denies platform but platforms martyrdom narrative
questions.answer: Denies platform but platforms martyrdom narrative

questions.q: Speaker view: sanitised square leads to?

title: Satirical Review: Tech Utopianism
audio_script: Critic: Silicon Valley's latest promise — that an app will 'disrupt' loneliness — is, with exquisite irony, being pitched by the very ecosystem that engineered it. The solution to a problem caused by substituting connection with connectivity is, apparently, more connectivity, albeit with a subscription. One is reminded of the old quip that the cover-up is worse than the crime, except here the cover-up is the business model.

options: App solves loneliness but ecosystem caused it
questions.answer: App solves loneliness but ecosystem caused it

title: Supreme Court Oral Argument
audio_script:
Justice: Counsel, your reading would render the savings clause a nullity — a textbook surplusage problem. How do you square that with the canon against superfluity?
Counsel: Your Honor, not a nullity but a narrow office: it preserves only claims that would otherwise abate, not those that would be preempted. The distinction, albeit subtle, is dispositive.

title: Literary Lecture: Unreliable Narrator
audio_script: Professor: The brilliance of Ishiguro's narrator is not that he lies, but that he deceives himself with such consummate politeness that we collude. The hedged recollections — 'perhaps it was', 'one might have thought' — are not lapses of memory but acts of self-preservation. To parse his account is to become complicit in the very repression he performs.

title: Geopolitics Briefing
audio_script: Analyst: The conventional framing of this conflict as a binary — autocracy versus democracy — collapses under scrutiny. The belligerents are not monoliths; patronage networks cut across ideological lines, and the war economy has created vested interests in perpetuation. Any settlement that ignores these granular realities, however normatively appealing, will be stillborn.

title: Philosophy: Moral Luck
audio_script: Philosopher: Nagel's problem of moral luck is vertiginous: two drivers, equally reckless, swerve identically, yet one, by luck, kills a child who darts into the road, the other does not. Our reactive attitudes — blame, guilt — track outcome, not just agency. If we accept that luck permeates agency itself — constitutive luck — then the very ground of moral assessment trembles.

options: Two equally reckless drivers, one kills by luck → blame tracks outcome
questions.answer: Two equally reckless drivers, one kills by luck → blame tracks outcome
